B1: multilayer perceptron on the mean-pooled vector

B1 is the reference model. The mean-pooled ESM-2 vector is standardised and passed through two blocks of a linear layer, batch normalisation (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015), a rectified linear unit and dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014), with widths 512 and 256. It is the model against which the contrastive term is tested, and, because the heads and the losses are shared with the other models, setting λ = 0 gives exactly the same network trained with the cross-entropy loss alone.

B2 applies three parallel one-dimensional convolutions with kernel sizes of 3, 5 and 7 residues to the adapted residue vectors, each followed by a rectified linear unit and a masked global maximum over positions. The kernels respond to local residue motifs, and the maximum makes the response independent of where in the peptide a motif occurs. This is the sequence-domain analogue of a convolutional image network.
B3: bidirectional long short-term memory network

B3 passes the adapted residue vectors through a two-layer bidirectional LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) using packed sequences, so that padding does not enter the recurrence, and uses the final forward and backward states of the top layer. It models the order of residues in both directions, which pooling discards.
B4: convolutional network followed by a bidirectional LSTM

B4 combines the two preceding ideas: a convolution extracts local motifs from the adapted residue vectors and a one-layer bidirectional LSTM models their order, with a masked maximum over positions of the recurrent outputs. The hybrid tests whether local motifs and residue order carry information that either alone does not.

B5 adds a learned positional embedding to the adapted residue vectors and applies a two-layer Transformer encoder with four attention heads (Vaswani et al., 2017) and a key-padding mask, followed by a masked mean over positions. The encoder layers are trained from scratch on top of the frozen language model features. The model tests whether attention among at most thirty residues helps at this data scale.

B6 replaces the mean in Equation 3.2 with a learned weighted average: a small network scores each residue and a masked softmax turns the scores into weights (Ilse et al., 2018). The pooled vector then enters the same 512–256 encoder as B1. Because everything after pooling is identical to B1, the comparison of B1 and B6 isolates the pooling step from the rest of the architecture.
